newsitem.title: INDIA: Britain's Major to see India's "Silicon Valley".
newsitem.headline: Britain's Major to see India's "Silicon Valley".

text.p: British Prime Minister John Major, ignoring election fever at home, was to fly to India's "Silicon Valley" on Friday after putting trade at the top of the agenda of his week-long trip to South Asia.
Major told some 6,000 Indian businessmen on Thursday in the eastern city of Calcutta that free trade was the only way to avoid economic disaster.
Accompanied by more than 50 top business executives, Major said Britain aimed to further increase trade with India, which doubled over the past four years to 3.5 billion sterling ($6 billion).
British and Indian companies signed three joint ventures on Thursday in Calcutta on the first stage of Major's trip that will also take him to neighbouring Bangladesh and Pakistan.

More agreements were expected on Friday, when Major was to hold talks with Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda on his official aircraft taking them to the southern city of Bangalore, capital of Deve Gowda's home state of Karnataka.
Bangalore is called the Silicon Valley of India because of its high concentration of software and high-technology firms.
The city is a showcase for Indian entrepreneurship and the home of numerous joint ventures with foreign firms.

Major on Thursday gently pressed India to push ahead with free-market economic reforms which were launched in 1991, saying the world's second most populous nation should lower tariffs on imports of consumer goods and open up its insurance sector.
Major, asked by businessmen whether India's leaders should forge ahead "recklessly" with privatisation or be cautious, said: "I wouldn't advise you to do it recklessly but do it, yes...Go ahead."
Major said Britain's experience with privatisation would be a key part of his talks with Deve Gowda.
Major is pinning his hopes for a general election victory on Britain's booming economy.

But with the final date for the election no more than four months away, Major's ruling Conservatives trailed the opposition by some 20 points and the ruling party has been unable to make inroads on that lead.
Senior Conservative sources have expressed surprise that Major should take a week out of a hectic domestic schedule so close to the election for an extended foreign trip.
But Major angrily dismissed suggestions that he should be focusing solely on the election, telling reporters travelling with him that the business of government had to go on.
His visit comes early in the year of India's 50th anniversary of independence from Britain.
Major also used his speech to Indian businessmen to make a thinly veiled reference to Indian voters at home who could hold the key to one or two marginal parliamentary seats.

Major praised the one-million-strong Indian community in Britain for its strong family values and its emphasis on educating the young, two themes he sees as central to the Conservative election campaign.
Major faced a hectic schedule in Bangalore of visits to joint Anglo-British ventures before leaving for Bangladesh later on Friday.
Major was to spend Saturday in Bangladesh before flying to Pakistan on Sunday.
